cards/1/q: Merge Sorted Array (#88): nums1 has length m + n, holding m sorted numbers and n free cells at the end; merge the sorted nums2 of length n into it. Why write from the end?
cards/1/options/0: The tail of nums1 is free: writing at position m + n − 1 and leftward never overwrites a number not yet read
cards/1/options/1: From the end there are fewer comparisons: O(n) instead of O(m + n)
cards/1/options/2: From the start also works without extra memory — the end is just the habit
cards/1/explain: Write the larger of the two tails at position w = i + j + 1, where i and j are the unread ends. While nums2 still has numbers, w > i: the write is always to the right of anything unread in nums1. It is the same trick as in squares of a sorted array: we know where the largest values are, so we start with them.
cards/1/wrong/1: The number of comparisons is the same — O(m + n) either way. The gain is in memory, not in steps.
cards/1/wrong/2: From the start, the very first write overwrites nums1[0] before it is compared; you would have to shift the tail or copy nums1 — O(m) memory or O(m · n) time.
cards/2/q: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (#26): keep one copy of each value at the front of the array and return how many there are.
cards/2/explain: Compare with the last kept value, nums[write − 1]: everything left of write is already the unique values in order, and in a sorted array equal values stand together. nums[read + 1] runs off the end on the last step. No swap is needed — dropped values are never needed again, plain assignment is enough. The answer is the new length, write.
cards/3/task: Step through Trapping Rain Water on [4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5]. The rig stops and asks how much water the code records: look at lmax, rmax and h[R].
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: L = 2 (height 0), R = 5 (height 5), lmax = 4, rmax = 0 — nothing on the right has been passed yet. How much water does the code record over bar 2?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: h[L] = 0 < h[R] = 5 — the left side is processed. There is guaranteed to be a wall of at least 5 on the right and 4 on the left, so the left one holds: 4 − 0 = 4. rmax = 0 only means “nothing passed on the right”, not “a wall of height 0”. h[R] = 5 is a guarantee, not the water level. On this array the right pointer never moves: the total is 9.
cards/4/q: The interviewer changes Two Sum II: there may be no answer, then return an empty array. On [2, 3, 4, 9], target = 8 the code returned [3, 3] — the same number twice. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/4/explain: When lo == hi both pointers sit on the same 4, and 4 + 4 = 8 counts as a pair. While an answer is guaranteed it is found before the pointers meet — so the bug only shows on an input with no answer. A pair means two different indices: while (lo < hi).
cards/5/q: Valid Palindrome II (#680): you may delete at most one character. Opposite pointers; on the first mismatch, check whether s[l + 1..r] or s[l..r − 1] is a palindrome. Complexity?
cards/5/explain: There is only one mismatch where we branch: each of the two checks is a plain opposite-pointer pass with no deletions allowed, O(n). At most three linear passes in total — O(n), O(1) memory.
cards/5/wrong/1: O(n²) would come from trying to delete every character in turn. Here there are only two candidates to delete — s[l] and s[r].
cards/5/wrong/2: There is no sorting or halving — only linear passes.
cards/6/q: A colleague writes Squares of a Sorted Array: l and r at the ends, the smaller of the two squares goes to the front of the answer. What ends up in res[0] on [-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]?
cards/6/explain: The ends are 16 and 100, the smaller is 16, and it goes to res[0], even though the smallest square is the 0 in the middle. The ends only guarantee the maximum; nobody knows where the minimum is. That is why the answer is filled from the end, taking the larger one.
cards/6/wrong/1: 0 is the correct answer to the problem, but this code only looks at the ends and has not reached the zero in the middle.
cards/6/wrong/2: 1 = (−1)² is not at an end either; the code picks the smaller of 16 and 100.
cards/7/q: Game code. What is true? Select all.
cards/7/options/0: Removing dead units from a List<Unit> when order does not matter: swap-remove from the end, O(1) per removal
cards/7/options/1: Rotating the data of a 5×3 room by 90°: you need a new 3×5 array
cards/7/options/2: The right neighbor in a flat grid is always i + 1
cards/7/options/3: Game of Life in an IJobParallelFor: read the old buffer, write the new one
cards/7/options/4: Container With Most Water: move the taller line so as not to lose height
cards/7/explain: Swap-remove from the end shifts no tail and moves an element that has already been checked. A rotated room swaps width and height. i + 1 on the right edge is the first cell of the next row; the edge is checked by x. Parallel jobs must not write where neighbors read — two buffers. In Container you move the shorter line: it is exhausted, the taller one is not.
cards/8/q: You are solving 3Sum out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/8/items/0: Clarify: values or indices, must triples be unique, the range of n
cards/8/items/1: Brute force over triples: O(n³), about 4.5·10⁹ for n = 3000
cards/8/items/2: Idea: sort, fix nums[i], find the pair with opposite pointers
cards/8/items/3: Duplicates: skip i if nums[i] == nums[i − 1], and move l and r past equal values after a hit
cards/8/items/5: Complexity: O(n²) time, memory is the in-place sort plus the answer
cards/8/items/6: Variations: 3Sum Closest, 4Sum in O(n³) with the sum in long
cards/8/explain: Sorting is allowed because values, not indices, are needed — worth saying out loud while clarifying. The example with two −1s checks the duplicate skipping.
